title: Dublin Flood Lab
summary: An interactive 3D scenario model exploring how river flows and coastal water levels could inundate terrain and streets along Dublin's Lower Liffey.
hero_alt: Lower Liffey terrain map with blue modelled flood depths around the river, Dublin Port, and low-lying areas during the 1% AEP design scenario
question: How could connected inundation develop through Dublin's Lower Liffey corridor as prescribed design river flows and coastal water levels rise, peak, and recede?
study_area: Islandbridge through the city quays to Alexandra Basin and Dublin Port; a 10 × 6 km study window in ITM, with a 5.08 km extracted Liffey centreline.
outcome: Three 49-frame design scenarios and three hypothetical sensitivity experiments on a 5 m terrain grid, with source-connected flood depths, street-threshold summaries, and a self-contained 3D timeline explorer.
role: Data research, terrain processing, reduced-complexity hydraulic approximation, scenario modelling, cartography, and interactive Three.js visualisation.
method_note: Headline values refer to the 1% AEP model scenario. They are simulated scenario summaries, not observed losses, official flood zones, or validated property-level estimates.

methods.title: Mosaic the terrain
methods.text: Query the GSI coverage service for the 23 intersecting OPW NASC tiles, download the 2 m bare-earth DTM, mosaic the study window, and aggregate it to a 5 m analysis grid in ITM. Nodata cells are audited and excluded from model statistics.

methods.title: Build the river and streets
methods.text: Assemble and orient the River Liffey centreline from OpenStreetMap between Islandbridge and Alexandra Basin. Densify it by chainage, then sample clipped OSM road geometries for exposure to modelled depths.

methods.title: Prescribe design boundaries
methods.text: Use OPW Appendix D Model 2C Qmed and peak-flow values for the 10%, 1%, and 0.1% AEP events. A normalised gamma-shaped hydrograph represents the rising and receding limbs. Dublin Port high/low predictions define a representative tidal cycle; published OPW NE_19 extreme levels define the coastal peaks.

methods.title: Run sensitivity experiments
methods.text: Route the 1% AEP upstream hydrograph through a conceptual reservoir using five-minute water-balance steps, or shift the prescribed coastal peak six hours earlier or later. Settings are explicit in flood-scenarios.json and do not represent observed operations or surge forecasts.

methods.title: Approximate the water surface
methods.text: Estimate normal depth with Manning's equation using n=0.04 from the OPW report, explicit channel-width assumptions, and a terrain-referenced bed profile. Combine the fluvial surface with a linearly attenuated coastal backwater surface. These are reduced-model assumptions, not a surveyed 1D/2D hydraulic model.

methods.title: Propagate connected flooding
methods.text: At each hour, subtract ground elevation from the chainage-interpolated water surface. Eight-neighbour connectivity retains only candidate cells connected to the river or estuary, preventing isolated low areas from flooding without a surface connection. Permanent water is excluded from land-area summaries.

methods.title: Export and explore
methods.text: Resample depth frames to a 20 m display grid, quantise terrain and depth textures, and simplify street vectors. A bundled Three.js renderer displays the same manifest used for the static maps and summaries. No data service is called by the published website.

formula_text: Depth d at scenario time t is the local water surface W, interpolated by river chainage s, minus ground elevation z. Only cells above the 0.05 m mapping threshold and connected to a source are retained. The model does not solve momentum or floodplain-storage equations.

maps.title: Three design events
maps.alt: Three maps comparing connected inundation at the peak boundary hour for 10%, 1%, and 0.1% AEP scenarios
maps.caption: The same terrain and scenario clock allow the three design events to be compared. These are reduced-model outputs at the peak boundary hour, not copies of official OPW flood-extent maps.

maps.title: What drives the timeline
maps.alt: Hydrographs of downstream design flow and coastal water level for three scenarios over 48 hours
maps.caption: The prescribed downstream flow hydrographs and coastal boundary series used by the model. Published coastal peaks include OPW's tide, surge, and seiching allowances; this project does not independently forecast those processes.

data.name: OPW NASC LiDAR DTM
data.provider: Geological Survey Ireland / Office of Public Works
data.details: Twenty-three intersecting 2 km tiles; 2 m bare-earth elevation, 2011 capture, ITM and OD Malin. Aggregated to 5 m for modelling and 20 m for display.
data.license: CC BY 4.0; required GSI & OPW attribution shown with the maps

data.name: Eastern CFRAM — Liffey Hydrology Report
data.details: Model 2C catchment and design-flow inputs from Table 4.4 and Appendix D. Used as published scenario parameters; no CFRAM flood-extent geometry is copied or redistributed.
data.license: Public technical report; source and table references retained

data.name: Eastern CFRAM — Liffey Hydraulics Report
data.details: Lower Liffey model scope, in-bank Manning n=0.04, and NE_19 coastal levels from Table 4.7.2: 2.67, 3.00, and 3.34 m OD Malin for the three AEP events.
data.license: Public technical report; source and table references retained

data.name: Dublin Port tide predictions
data.provider: Marine Institute — Irish National Tide Gauge Network
data.details: High/low predictions for 14–18 January 2027 define a representative 12.42-hour tidal cycle in OD Malin. The model adds a prescribed residual to match published OPW coastal design peaks; this is not a storm-surge forecast.

data.name: River Liffey and Dublin streets
data.details: Bounding-box extract of river ways and road geometries, transformed to ITM. Street summaries use a 0.05 m modelled-depth threshold and do not represent official closures. Distributed OSM-derived vectors remain under ODbL.

implemented_experiments.title: Conceptual reservoir routing
implemented_experiments.text: Route the 1% AEP upstream design hydrograph through a hypothetical 30 million m³ store with explicit release rules and five-minute water-balance steps. Storage and release are shown in the viewer; no ESB operating data are implied.

implemented_experiments.title: Compound-event timing
implemented_experiments.text: Move the prescribed 1% AEP coastal peak six hours before or after the river peak. These scenarios isolate timing sensitivity without claiming to model observed surge, tide–surge interaction, or coastal hydrodynamics.

future_implementations.title: 2D hydrodynamics
future_implementations.text: Add a calibrated local-inertial or shallow-water solver with channel bathymetry, spatial roughness, volume conservation, velocity outputs, and more realistic floodplain storage and recession.

future_implementations.title: Bridges & culverts
future_implementations.text: Couple surveyed cross-sections, opening dimensions, and invert levels to the terrain model. Add blockage scenarios only when structural geometry and reusable survey data support them.

future_implementations.title: Sewer surcharge
future_implementations.text: Integrate a dual-drainage network with pipe diameters, inverts, gullies, outfalls, capacities, and initial storage rather than inferring underground behaviour from surface elevation.

future_implementations.title: Groundwater
future_implementations.text: Add aquifer geometry, permeability, groundwater observations, and subsurface–surface exchange through a suitable hydrogeological model.

future_implementations.title: Defence failure
future_implementations.text: Use surveyed crests for overtopping and document breach timing and growth explicitly. Separate hypothetical breach scenarios from evidence-based failure predictions.

future_implementations.title: Observed reservoir operations
future_implementations.text: Replace the conceptual router with ESB storage, gate settings, operating rules, and observed release series. Keep scripted releases distinct from predicted operator decisions.

future_implementations.title: Dynamic surge & compound events
future_implementations.text: Move beyond prescribed coastal levels and timing shifts by coupling observed or forecast surge, tide–surge interaction, coastal hydrodynamics, and uncertainty with the fluvial model.

caveat: This reduced model does not resolve velocity, momentum, dynamic floodplain storage, culvert or bridge blockage, sewer surcharge, groundwater, defence failure, waves, or storm-surge dynamics. Reservoir routing and coastal timing experiments use hypothetical prescribed settings, not ESB decisions or surge forecasts. Terrain age, nodata areas, datum handling, normal-depth assumptions, and resampling all affect results. Consult floodinfo.ie and qualified professionals for official information; never use this visualisation for emergency, property, insurance, planning, or road-safety decisions.
